# Falling bodies and projectiles (`falling_bodies`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by mechanical_clock, symbolic_algebra
- Core idea: Apart from air resistance, all bodies fall at the same rate whatever their weight: a heavy and a light ball dropped together from a tower land together. The speed grows steadily (about 10 m/s more every second) and the distance grows with the square of the time: about 5 m in the first second, 20 m after two, 45 m after three. It can be shown slowly by rolling a ball down a grooved ramp and marking positions at equal beats: the gaps go as 1, 3, 5, 7. A thrown or fired body keeps its forward motion while it falls, so its path is a parabola, and the longest range on level ground is near 45 degrees, less for fast shot in air.
- Pitfalls:
  - Dropping a feather or paper to 'prove' it and being refuted by air resistance; use two dense balls
  - Citing the Leaning Tower experiment as fact (it rests only on Viviani's late account)
  - Saying speed is proportional to distance fallen (Galileo's own first error); it is proportional to time
  - Applying the vacuum parabola to cannon shot, which falls far short
- History: greece: 4th c. BC – Aristotle: heavier bodies fall faster in proportion to weight; egypt: c. 530 AD – John Philoponus (Byzantine Alexandria) reports that unequal weights fall in nearly equal times; islamic: 12th c. – Abu'l-Barakat al-Baghdadi describes acceleration of fall as accumulating impetus; europe: 14th c. Merton scholars and Oresme, mean-speed theorem; 1537 Tartaglia on gunnery; 1551 de Soto calls fall uniformly accelerated; 1586 Stevin's drop test at Delft; c. 1604–1609 Galileo's ramp experiments, published 1638
- Read:
  - Galileo Galilei, Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze (1638)
  - Stillman Drake, Galileo at Work: His Scientific Biography (1978)
